title: Your four foundations
hook: a sitting that moves through body, feeling, mind and dhammas

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven years, or seven days. Your line was even seven days. If you made a small promise, today is day one of it. Day two hundred sixty-six, the last day in the Satipatthana Sutta.

Three weeks ago, we opened a text that a great deal of the world's mindfulness traces back to. We walked through it one section at a time: the breath, the postures, the bag of grain, the charnel ground, the second arrow, the five visitors, the six doors, the seven factors. Today there's nothing new to learn. Today you get to put the whole thing together, the way it was meant to be used: not as a list, but as one sitting. Today: your four foundations.
screen: `THREE WEEKS IN ONE TEXT.` → `NOTHING NEW TODAY.` → `ONE SITTING, ALL FOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole sutta in one breath. Satipatthana: one way, four doors. The refrain: ardent and gentle. First foundation, the body. Knowing the breath, like the turner at the lathe. The chorus: it arises, it passes. The postures: I know I'm sitting. Clear knowing: even this. The parts: a bag of grain. The elements: four elements. The charnel ground: this body too. Second foundation, feelings: pleasant, painful, neither, and one arrow, not two. Third foundation, the mind: know the mind, and just know it. Fourth foundation, dhammas: the hindrances, it came, it went; five heaps; the fetter at the door; seven factors; and the four truths, know it as it is. And the promise: even seven days. It sounds like a lot. But look at how the four fit together. They move from the most solid to the most subtle. The body is easy to find: you can always feel your seat. Feelings are a little quicker, a flicker of pleasant or painful. The mind is subtler again, its whole weather. And dhammas are the patterns running through all of it. Each one is a place to stand. On a scattered day, you might only manage the first. On a clear day, you might move through all four. Teachers often compare them to four legs of a table, or four gates into one city. The practice isn't to master all four at once. It's to know that wherever you are, one of them is right under your feet.
screen: `THE WHOLE SUTTA IN ONE BREATH.` · `BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, DHAMMAS.` · `FROM MOST SOLID TO MOST SUBTLE.` · `ONE IS ALWAYS UNDER YOUR FEET.` · then, large: `FOUR PLACES TO STAND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. We'll take about thirty seconds for each foundation. Body: feel the breath, long or short, and the shape of your posture. Feelings: what's pleasant here, what's unpleasant, what's neither? Mind: what's the weather, tight or open, scattered or gathered? Dhammas: is a hindrance here, or a factor of awakening, maybe a little calm, a little curiosity? Then rest wherever you find yourself. If you'd like the full version, fifteen minutes, try it some quiet morning this week. The bell holds the time.
Your four foundations. Body, feelings, mind and dhammas: four places to set mindfulness down, from the most solid to the most subtle.
Your line: four places to stand. Today, whenever you feel lost, find the body first: your feet, your seat, your breath. Tomorrow a new part begins: the Heart Sutra. Day two hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Many practitioners do a sitting that moves through body, feelings, mind and dhammas in turn, and on retreats in the Theravada and insight traditions all four are practiced throughout the day, in sitting, walking and daily tasks.

match.prompt: match each foundation to one of its lines.

myth: the four foundations move from most subtle to most solid
they move from most solid, the body, to most subtle, the dhammas.
the practice is to master all four at once
it's to know that one of them is always under your feet.
the body is often the easiest place to start
you can always feel your seat and your breath.

fork.setup: it's a scattered, busy day and you have one minute. which foundation is the easiest place to stand?
options: the body: feel your feet, your seat, your breath.
the dhammas: analyze the five heaps.
none: wait for a calmer day.
fork.reveal: the body is the most solid of the four and always available. on a scattered day, it's enough.

original.note: Pali satipaṭṭhāna: the foundations, or establishing, of mindfulness.

trapdoor: what you thought: the four foundations are four separate meditations to choose from.
what it means: four places to stand, from solid to subtle, all part of one path.
what a scholar hears: the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta (SN 47) collects many shorter suttas on the four, including the simile of the quail who stays safe in its own ancestral territory.

notes: Week 38 end and close of 'The Satipatthana Sutta' (days 246–266): the teach names the carries of days 246–265; confirm.
The 'most solid to most subtle' ordering is a common teaching framing, not from the sutta itself.
Quail simile in SN 47.6 (Sakuṇagghi Sutta): confirm reference.
The practice is sized to the app's 2-minute sit; the outline's fifteen minutes is offered as an optional longer sit.
